title: Heavy bleeding from a wound
askedAs: someone is bleeding a lot
how do I stop bad bleeding
blood is spurting from a cut on their leg
when do I use a tourniquet
summary: Heavy bleeding can kill in a few minutes, so act on it before anything else.
steps: Uncover the wound so you can see where the blood is coming from.
Press hard and directly on the spot that is bleeding most, with gauze or the cleanest cloth you have.

If it is an arm or leg and pressure is not stopping it, put a tourniquet on 2 to 3 inches above the wound, on bare skin, and tighten it until the bleeding stops. Expect it to hurt; that means it is tight enough.
No tourniquet? Make one from a strip of cloth at least 1.5 inches wide and a stick: tie it around the limb, tie the stick into the knot, and twist until the bleeding stops.
For a deep wound where a tourniquet cannot go (neck, armpit, groin), pack the wound tightly with gauze or clean cloth and hold firm pressure for at least 3 minutes.
Once it stops, wrap a bandage firmly over the dressing to hold the pressure.
dont: Don't loosen or take off a tourniquet once it is on. Leave that to medical staff.
Don't put a tourniquet around the neck.
Don't wrap a bandage so tight that there's no pulse below it. The skin below should stay pink and warm with a pulse; if it doesn't, loosen and re-tie the bandage.
getHelp: This is an emergency. Get the person to medical care as fast as you can. A tourniquet is safest for under two hours.
reviewerNote: Sources disagree on two points. WHO BEC (2018) says to raise a bleeding limb above the heart, and ATP 3-50.21 (2018) says to hold direct pressure for 30 minutes before a pressure dressing. The pressure-bandage line now follows ATP 4-02.11 p.65 and p.67 word for word.

title: A bandage soaking through with blood
askedAs: the bandage is soaked with blood
blood is coming through the dressing
should I change a bloody bandage
summary: Leave the soaked dressing on. Add more on top and press harder.
steps: Keep the first dressing where it is. Pulling it off tears away the clot that is starting to form.
Put another pad or more gauze straight on top of it.
Press firmly on the source of the bleeding again.
A bandage that keeps soaking through means the bleeding is serious. If it is an arm or leg and it will not stop, use a tourniquet (see heavy bleeding).
When it stops, wrap a bandage firmly over everything to hold it in place.
dont: Don't take off the soaked dressing.
getHelp: Bleeding that soaks through a bandage counts as life-threatening. Get medical help as soon as you can.

title: Twisted or sprained ankle, or a strained muscle
askedAs: I twisted my ankle on the trail
my knee is swollen after I rolled it
how do I treat a sprain
I pulled a muscle
summary: Treat it with RICE: rest, ice, compression, elevation.
steps: Rest: stop using the injured joint.
Ice: use cold compresses or an improvised ice pack on and off, for up to 48 hours.
Compression: wrap or splint it to keep it stable. On an ankle, leave the boot on unless the foot's circulation looks cut off.
Elevation: raise the injured part.
A torn muscle or bad sprain can look like a break. Signs to watch for are a pop at the time of injury, swelling, bruising and not being able to move it.
dont: Don't wrap it so tight the foot or hand below goes numb, pale or bluish. Loosen it if that happens.
getHelp: If they cannot move it, or it might be broken, splint it and get it checked.
reviewerNote: Our tuning answer sheet (fa-ankle-01) says to remove footwear. The Army survival manual says to leave the boot on a sprained ankle unless circulation is compromised, and this card follows the manual. The answer sheet may need fixing. Quotes no longer carry the 'R-Rest' letter prefixes; the corpus cleaner now strips them at the next rebuild.

title: Snakebite
askedAs: snake bite first aid
my friend got bitten by a snake
what do I do for a snake bite
should I suck the venom out
summary: Keep them still and calm, and get to medical care. Antivenom is the real treatment.
steps: Keep the person as still and calm as you can. Moving around and panicking speed up how fast the venom spreads.
Take off rings, watches and anything tight near the bite before it swells.
Keep the bitten arm or leg slightly below the level of the heart if you can.
Wash the bite gently with mild soap and water.
Cover it with a clean bandage that is snug but not tight, and splint the limb so it stays still.
Note the time of the bite. Watch their breathing and be ready to do CPR.
dont: Don't cut the bite open or try to suck out the venom.
Don't put a tourniquet on the limb.
Don't put ice on it.
Don't try to catch or kill the snake. You risk a second bite. A photo from a safe distance is fine.
getHelp: Get medical help right away. Most snakebites are not deadly, but hospitals have the antivenom and you don't.
reviewerNote: WHO BEC describes a firm pressure bandage up the whole limb, but only for snakes whose venom affects the nerves (like coral snakes), and says it is NOT recommended for snakes whose venom damages tissue near the bite (like rattlesnakes). A hiker can't tell which, so this card uses the snug bandage and splint from ATP 4-02.11 instead.

title: Someone is choking
askedAs: someone is choking
my friend can't breathe, something is stuck in their throat
how do I do the Heimlich
choking and can't talk
summary: If they can cough or talk, let them cough. If they can't breathe, cough or speak, act now: five back blows, then abdominal thrusts until it comes out.
steps: Ask if they are choking. If they can speak or cough strongly, encourage them to keep coughing and don't interfere.
If they can't breathe, speak or cough, or their breathing makes a high-pitched sound, call for help and act now.
Give five back blows first: lean them forward and strike firmly between the shoulder blades with the heel of your hand.

Then give abdominal thrusts: stand behind them and wrap your arms around their waist. Make a fist and put the thumb side against the middle of the belly, just above the belly button and well below the breastbone. Grab the fist with your other hand and thrust quickly inward and upward.
Make each thrust a separate, distinct push, and keep going until the object comes out or they pass out.
If they're pregnant, very large, or have a belly wound, use chest thrusts instead: arms under their armpits, fist in the middle of the breastbone, and thrust inward.
If they pass out, call for help, lay them on their back and start CPR. Each time you open the airway to give breaths, look in the mouth and take the object out only if you can see it.
dont: Don't give back blows or thrusts while they can still cough or speak.
Don't sweep your fingers blindly through their mouth. It can push the object deeper.
getHelp: For an infant, lay them face down along your arm or thigh with the head low and give five back blows, then turn them over and give five chest pushes with two fingers.
reviewerNote: Now follows ATP 4-02.11 (2026): five back blows, then abdominal thrusts continued until the object is out or they pass out. WHO BEC (2018) alternates five and five; both use back blows and abdominal thrusts, and the newer order is used. The infant steps are from WHO, since the Army manual has none.

title: Hypothermia: shivering, confused, too cold
askedAs: my friend is shivering and confused
fell in a cold creek and can't stop shivering
how do I warm someone up
signs of hypothermia
summary: Get them out of the cold, get them dry, wrap them up, and handle them gently. Severe hypothermia needs a hospital.
steps: Watch for the signs: uncontrollable shivering, cold pale skin, slurred speech, clumsiness, sleepiness and confusion. If the shivering stops while they are still cold, it is getting worse, not better.
Get them out of the wind and cold.
Replace wet clothes with dry ones.
Put insulation under them as well as over them. The cold ground pulls heat out fast.
Wrap them from head to toe, leaving the face uncovered.
If they are awake and can swallow, give them warm, sweet drinks slowly.
Move them as little as possible and handle them gently. For severe cases, skin-to-skin contact inside a sleeping bag can help.
dont: Don't give alcohol, caffeine or tobacco.
getHelp: Hypothermia is a medical emergency. Evacuate as soon as you can, with the person lying down. Rewarming someone who is severely hypothermic should be done by medical professionals.

title: Staying warm on a cold night
askedAs: staying warm overnight below freezing
how do I stay warm overnight
how do I avoid hypothermia while camping
my clothes are wet and it's getting cold
summary: Get off the cold ground, stay dry, block the wind, and wear loose layers.
steps: Put insulation between you and the ground. A sleeping pad works, or use spare clothes, dry grass, ferns or pine boughs piled at least 12 inches thick. Fluff it up between uses.
Stay dry. Wet clothing pulls heat away up to 25 times faster than dry clothing. Dry damp clothes near your body or at a safe distance from a fire.
Get out of the wind. Moving air strips away the warm layer next to your skin. Face a shelter's opening sideways to the wind, at 90 degrees to it.
Wear several loose layers instead of one thick one, and cover your head, neck, hands and feet.
Don't overheat while setting up. Sweat soaks your clothes and chills you later, so open a layer if you start sweating.
Drink warm fluids and keep hydrated.
dont: Don't wear tight clothing or boots. They cut off circulation and invite cold injuries.
Don't use candles or stoves in a closed-up shelter without a vent. They make carbon monoxide.
getHelp: If anyone starts shivering uncontrollably, gets clumsy or confused, treat it as hypothermia.
reviewerNote: Your note: wind angle now stated as 'sideways to the wind, at 90 degrees to it'.

title: Immersion foot (trench foot): cold, wet, numb feet

summary: Feet that stay wet and cold for a long time can get immersion foot, also called trench foot. Warm and dry them gently.
steps: At first the feet feel cold and numb, and they may burn or shoot with pain as they warm up. Later, the skin turns bluish and pale, the pulse in the foot weakens, and blisters and swelling appear.
Get out of the wet and cold.
Take off wet boots and socks and let the feet dry.
Warm them gradually with warm air.
Raise the feet a little to help with swelling.
Put on clean, dry, loose socks, and protect the feet from knocks. Avoid walking on them.
dont: Don't rub or massage the feet.
Don't warm them with a fire or other direct heat. Numb feet burn without you noticing.
getHelp: Advanced immersion foot can turn to gangrene, so get it seen by a doctor. Prevent it by changing into dry socks during the day and drying your feet every day.

summary: Frozen skin looks pale, waxy or hard and goes numb. Rewarm it gently in warm water, never over a fire.
steps: Watch for it on fingers, toes, ears, nose and cheeks. The skin suddenly goes white, then tingles. When the area stops hurting, frostbite has set in. Frozen skin feels hard, waxy or wooden.
Chilblains (red, swollen, tender, itchy skin after repeated cold exposure) usually get better if you warm the area with body heat. Don't rub it.
For frostbite, thaw the area in warm water between 99 and 109°F (37 to 43°C).
Loosen anything tight, keep the area warm, and protect it from more cold or knocks.
Once it has thawed, cover it with a clean dressing and raise it to reduce swelling.
dont: Don't rub or massage it.
Don't hold it near a fire to thaw it. Numb skin burns badly without you feeling it.
getHelp: All frostbite needs to be seen by a doctor, even if it looks mild.

title: Burns

how do I treat a burn

burn with blisters
summary: Stop the burning, then work out how deep the burn is. Surface and blistering burns get cool water; deep burns get only a brief cool compress and a moist cover.
steps: If clothing is on fire: stop, drop and roll. Don't run.

Work out the kind of burn. Red and painful with no blisters: a surface (first-degree) burn. Blisters and swelling: a partial-thickness (second-degree) burn. Leathery, dry skin that looks white, brown or black, and may not hurt at all: a full-thickness (third-degree) burn.
Surface burn: soak it in cool water to ease the pain.
Blistering burn: take off rings and tight clothing before it swells, cool it with cool running water or moist cloths until the pain eases, then cover it with a clean, dry, non-stick dressing.
Deep burn: cool it only briefly with cool, wet compresses, leave any charred clothing that's stuck to it, and cover it with cool, moist, clean dressings.
For any serious burn, keep them warm, watch for shock, and have them drink water to replace lost fluid.
dont: Don't use ice or ice water. It damages the skin more.
Don't soak a deep burn in cold water.
Don't put butter, grease, ointments or home remedies on a burn.
Don't pull off clothing that is stuck to the burn.
getHelp: Deep burns need medical care right away. So do burns to the face or neck, or soot in the mouth or nose, which can mean the airway is burned.

title: Heat exhaustion and heat stroke
askedAs: my friend is dizzy and sweating a lot in the heat
signs of heat stroke
what's the difference between heat exhaustion and heat stroke
someone overheated on the hike
summary: Heat exhaustion means heavy sweating, weakness and dizziness: cool them and give water. Heat stroke means hot, dry skin and confusion: it is an emergency, so cool them fast.
steps: Heat exhaustion looks like heavy sweating, cool clammy skin, weakness, dizziness, headache, nausea and cramps.
For heat exhaustion: move them into shade, have them lie down with their legs raised a little, loosen tight clothing, put cool wet cloths on the neck, face and armpits, and fan them.
Have them sip cool water slowly. If they don't improve within 30 minutes, get help.
Heat stroke looks like confusion, hot dry skin with little or no sweating, a fast strong pulse, and sometimes seizures or collapse. Heat exhaustion can turn into it.
For heat stroke: cool them as fast as you can. Put them in cool water if possible. Otherwise soak their clothes and focus on the groin, armpits, back and neck, and fan them.
Watch their breathing and pulse, and start CPR if they stop.
dont: Don't give alcohol or caffeine.
getHelp: Heat stroke is a medical emergency. Call for help right away and keep cooling them while you wait.

title: Making water safe to drink
askedAs: treating creek or lake water
how do I purify water
purifying water without boiling
how long do I boil water
summary: Treat any water from a lake, stream, pond or spring before drinking it. Clear muddy water first, then boil it or treat it with tablets, iodine or bleach.
steps: Muddy or cloudy water: filter it through cloth, or let it seep into a hole dug beside the source, first. That makes it clearer, but you still have to purify it.
Boil it: bring it to a rolling boil for 1 minute. Above about 5,000 feet, boil it for 3 minutes.
Can't boil? Use purification tablets and follow the instructions on the packet. Check they haven't expired.
Tincture of iodine (2%): 5 drops per quart, or 10 if the water is cloudy or cold. Wait 30 minutes, or 60 if it's cold and cloudy.
Household bleach: the manual's amount is 2 drops per quart for 5.25% bleach, then wait 30 minutes (60 if the water is cold and cloudy). Bleach strength varies, so check the label.
After chemicals, open the cap and rinse the threads with treated water before drinking from the bottle.
dont: Don't add drink mix until the treatment time is over.
Don't rely on a filter alone. Most filters don't remove viruses.
If the water might contain fuel, pesticides or other chemicals, don't drink it. Boiling and disinfecting don't remove chemicals. Find another source.

summary: Look before you cross: pick a shallow stretch that splits into several narrow channels, angle downstream across the current, and use a pole on the upstream side.
steps: Find a high spot first and look along the river for the best place to cross.

In fast water, use a strong pole about 3 inches thick and 7 to 8 feet long. Plant it firmly on the upstream side, lean on it, and move one foot or the pole at a time.
In a group, cross together holding the pole side by side: heaviest person downstream, lightest upstream.

If you are swept away in fast, shallow water, lie on your back with your feet downstream and up, and steer with your hands. In deep, swift water, swim with the current, angling toward the shore, not against it.

summary: A few knots cover most needs: two half hitches or a round turn to tie to a tree, a square knot to join two ropes, and an overhand or figure-eight to stop an end.
steps: To tie a line to a tree or pole: take a round turn around it, then two half hitches around the line. It holds under heavy load and doesn't jam. For something quick and light, two half hitches alone will do, and a clove hitch also works.
To join two ropes of the same thickness: a square knot. Check that each end lies alongside its own rope; if not, it's a granny knot, which slips.
To stop the end of a rope slipping through: tie an overhand knot, or a figure-eight for a bigger knot.
Line every knot up neatly and pull it tight. A messy knot can lose half its strength or come undone.
Need thin cord? Paracord pulls apart into an outer cover and inner strands you can use as fishing line, thread or lashing.

Testing a plant for cord: pull it to test its strength, twist and roll the fibres between your fingers, then tie an overhand knot and tighten it gently. If it survives all that without breaking, it will work. Braid several strands together for more strength.
dont: Don't trust a half hitch on its own. It can undo itself when there's no load on it.

getHelp: Both are emergencies. Get medical help as fast as you possibly can.

summary: Don't run. Stay calm, talk to it in a low voice, and back away slowly sideways. If it attacks: fight back against a black bear, play dead against a grizzly.
steps: Stay calm. Most bears do not want to attack you and most encounters end without anyone getting hurt.
Talk to the bear calmly in a low voice so it knows you are a person. Stand your ground and slowly wave your arms.
Pick up small children right away. Stay together as a group and make yourselves look as big as you can.
If the bear isn't moving, move away slowly and sideways so you can keep watching it. Leave it a way out.
If the bear follows, stop and hold your ground. A bear may charge and turn away at the last second.
If you carry bear spray, it is made for exactly this: an aggressive, charging or attacking bear.
If a black bear attacks: don't play dead. Get to a car or building if you can; if not, fight back, aiming at its face and muzzle.

If a grizzly (brown bear) attacks: leave your pack on and play dead. Lie flat on your stomach, hands clasped behind your neck, legs spread. Stay still until it leaves. If the attack keeps going, fight back hard at its face.
If any bear attacks you in your tent, or follows you and then attacks, fight back. Don't play dead.

Don't scream or make sudden movements. Never make high-pitched sounds.

Don't drop your pack or let the bear get your food.
Never get between a mother bear and her cubs.
getHelp: If anyone is hurt, treat their wounds and get medical help. Report the encounter to a park ranger as soon as you can.

summary: Don't go closer or try to put it out. Leave by a route away from the fire and the way the wind is blowing, and report it. If it reaches you, get to the spot with the least to burn and lie face down, covered.
steps: Don't go closer to look, and don't try to put the fire out yourself.
Note where the fire is as best you can and report it to a ranger, or call 911.
Leave the area. Fires mostly travel with the wind, so pick a route out in another direction, away from the fire.
Follow directions from fire crews and rangers, and stay out of closed areas.
In smoke, slow down and take it easy, and rest where the air is clearer. Eye irritation, a sore throat, wheezing and coughing mean the smoke is getting to you.
If the fire is closing in and you can't get away, go to the place with the least to burn: bare ground, rock, a road, or a large lake. Stay out of canyons, gullies that act like chimneys, and saddles.

In the backcountry, find a dip in the ground with little to burn. Clear away what plants you can while the fire is still coming, then lie face down in it and cover yourself. Stay down until the fire passes.
If a road is close, lie face down in the ditch on the uphill side. Cover yourself with anything that will shield you from the heat.
If you are in a car, stay in it rather than running on foot. Park away from trees and brush, close the windows and vents, get on the floor and cover up with a blanket or coat.
dont: Don't try to outrun the fire once it is close.
Don't drive through heavy smoke.
Don't light any fire, even to signal.
getHelp: Call 911 or send an SOS as soon as you know a fire is near you, and again if you are cut off or anyone has real trouble breathing. Anyone with burns: see the burns card.
